title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service's note-taking application allegedly records virtual meetings without the knowledge or consent of all participants. The system reportedly joins meetings automatically when a host with an account links their calendar, captures audio, and then uses those recordings to train its AI models. This represents a failure to obtain informed consent before collecting and repurposing data from conversations where participants had no reason to expect they were being recorded.

The deployment failure occurred at the point where the system was made available to users without adequate safeguards or transparency. Participants in meetings had no clear notification that recording was occurring or that their speech would be used for model training. What it would have taken to catch this: requiring explicit, separate consent from all meeting participants before recording, not just the host, and providing clear notice before joining a call.

It is not established whether the company's stated practices around consent checkboxes and de-identification actually match what occurred, whether participants were harmed, or what the legal outcome will be. The lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding of wrongdoing.

summary:
# Summary

A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based transcription company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer, claims the company's Otter Notebook service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without alerting participants, then shares these recordings with Otter to improve its artificial intelligence systems in violation of state and federal privacy laws. The company serves approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since 2016.

The lawsuit argues that Otter's software can automatically join meetings and record conversations without obtaining consent from participants, particularly when the meeting host has an Otter account linked to their calendar. While Otter's privacy policy claims it receives explicit permission through user checkboxes and de-identifies audio before training its systems, the suit contends the company provides no transparent explanation of its anonymization process. The case follows several high-profile complaints from users, including an incident where confidential investor details were recorded and shared, potentially derailing a business deal.
